[B][u]The Communist Agitators[/u][/b]

Ever since the Majlis outlawed communism as an prohibited ideology, its adherents were forced underground. Student groups, formerly the main stronghold of communist ideology, were raided and had their members placed under lengthy investigations. The leaders of these groups were placed on the National Security Register, the nationwide database containing all citizens and foreigners involved in terrorism against Dhornaper and her allies, while lesser individuals were put on the police database as potential individuals of interest. While such harsh measures enforced so speedily were enough to shock the communists underground and prevent them from causing mischief in the short term, the communists were unlikely to abandon their sincerely held beliefs so easily.

Indeed, communists continued to meet in secret and discuss their ideologies through encrypted Internet communication platforms and anonymous Internet forums. The most vigilant and militant communists eventually ended up coordinating and forming a core of aggressive and hardened agitators. From this core came the most aggressive opposition to the government. Although most of their writings stayed obscure, one particularly fiery article made its way public and became widely shared:

[I]"The dictatorship of Fereydun Shah has proclaimed that communism is an ideology equal to the barbarism of fascism and its cousin, ethnonationalism. By putting it on such a level, the Shah has declared it an oppressor, a colonialist force, and a deadly idea that must be exterminated lest Dhornaper fall into the grips of tyranny.

With this, Fereydun Shah has imitated the imperialists he moves to accelerate the doom of. By his own greed for power and adulation, he is attempting to supress the worker's revolution so his power may remain strong. He perpetuates the supremacy of the bourgeoisie, as that is his power base, and subjects the proletariat masses to tyranny every day. His outlawing of communism is his fear of a worker's revolution. He knows it approaches and he is afraid of the spectre that haunts him. The dichotomy is stark for the proletariat: exploitation under the parvenu Shah and his bourgeoisie power base or liberation under a proletariat revolution. The revolution cannot be suppressed.

Fereydun Shah demonstrates the fundamental truth of liberal democracy. The opium it feeds to the workers, that their plight is temporary and will improve under a harmonious social contract with the bourgeoisie, is a myth. All liberal democracies will degenerate. Fereydun Shah has become a ruler far more absolute than anything Jalaludin Shah or Ayub Khan could have dreamt of. He condemns communism as a mortal threat to Dhornaper as it is a mortal threat to his absolutist reign. Only communism is capable of overthrowing the oppressive regime of the bourgeoisie and creating a truly equal society."[/i]

It spread like wildfire. Underground communist groups and "political clubs" began sharing it and soon it reached the wider public. At this point the pamphlet couldn't be contained and the government lifted the censorship on reporting but established certain key "facts" media outlets had to report along side it:

[List=1]
[*]The pamphlet bore inspiration from Socialist International and Stuipendian literature, banned in Dhornaper for calling for the overthrow of the government.
[*]The authors of the pamphlet were likely members of a proscribed communist group which had thrown molotov cocktails at police stations.
[*]The Ministry of Internal Affairs is investigating the proscribed groups and tracking down their underground members.
[/list]

The pamphlet forced the Ministry of Internal Affairs to reveal its hand quickly. Several servers hosted on the dark web, which had been hacked with help from the newly formed cyber defence centre, had already been using malicious code that exploited bugs in older browsers to gain access to user devices. While plenty of users were identified, the more vigilant users remained impervious and anonymous. Nevertheless, the Ministry of Internal Affairs' counter-terrorism teams raided homes in night raids and bagged dozens of communists while the regular police raided already known persons of interest. It was one of the most complex operations in Dhora policing history.

To further enhance the image of the police, all suspects were paraded in Shar as they made their way to the central prison with people and the media taking pictures and watching them pass by. Given the magnitude of the crimes they're accused of: treason, plotting terror attacks, and being part of proscribed groups or having proscribed literature, they would remain in custody until the courts deal with them. The Ministry of Internal Affairs had its image restored and buffed up after the embarrassing proliferation of incendiary literature.

[spoiler=Expansion]
[i][b]1885 Expansion to the Eastern South of Argos.[/b]

The expansion of Argos in the direction of east and south between 1885 and 1887 marked a shift in the regions monetary objectives and the extent of their reach. What began as a series of small business trips quickly turned into a large-scale migration of people, workers, and leaders of the factories and mines, all in the hope of attaining new riches. The thick tropical forests, once thought of as hurdles, had now become the new opportunities. The first officially sanctioned expedition ventured out of the trade routes and into the heavily wooded southeastern frontiers on January 30, 1885.
 The initial intention of the people in the region had been to expand the trade routes and establish new connections with the new resources. However, the results of the survey expeditions sent out by the prospectors and geologists quickly changed the intentions of the people. The former found gold and silver deposits in the riverbeds and hills, while the latter found evidence of deeper deposits. The interest in the region was immediate and strong. The region may have had a lot of challenges, including the thick forests that obstructed the sun and the rains that made the routes muddy. However, the promise of riches kept the people moving. The camps set up by the people became the foundation of the new expansion routes.
By mid-1885, logging had really begun. The forest, which had previously been a hindrance, had now become one of the areas main advantages. Hardwood trees were cut faster and faster, providing much-needed wood. Sawmills were built near the rivers, which were then used to help transport these goods. Rivers played a vital role in moving these goods. This use of wood was only the beginning of economic growth, though, and with it came a big change to the environment.
As time went by, farming began to take place. The land, which had previously been so well suited to planting, was now perfect for planting due to its richness. Investors quickly took advantage of this, using their land to grow much-needed crops. Coffee was planted up on the hills, while banana trees were planted in the lower, wetter parts of the land. Indigo was planted, providing much needed dye for clothing. Coca was also planted, due to its profitability, and many people around the world needed coca.
With all of these changes, there was a need for more labor. More people were employed to assist, though some were forcibly taken there for the sake of economic growth. This economic growth, though providing money, also led to a class system, making people more unequal than before. The most important discovery, however, was yet to come. Later in 1885, people began drilling for water but instead found oil beneath the forest floor. After conducting more surveys, it was realized that there were large amounts of oil and gas in the area. This changed the entire idea of expansion. What was once a resource frontier is now an important area of industry. In early 1886, the drilling began. Simple drilling machines were installed, and soon more infrastructure was put in place for oil and gas drilling.
 Roads were cut through the forest for the transportation of machines, and pipelines were being connected for oil and gas drilling. Oil attracted more investors, engineers, and administrators, each seeking to gain from the area's potential. This industry, though, also led to more organization and control. Administrative districts were created for better control of the area. Authorities also sent security personnel for the maintenance of peace, especially in areas where people were displaced. Tensions rose as expansion reached areas already occupied by people. This led to conflicts, which were often resolved through force and annexation.
The expansion had an impact economically despite the challenges. For instance, the trade routes went deeper into the continent. Resources that had been isolated were now connected with the global economy. There was an increase in the export of timber, agriculture products, and other raw materials. This boosted the economy of the area. The ports and trade centers became busier. The influx of wealth helped the area grow and develop. 

However, the changes came with a cost. The environment reflected the impact of human activity. For instance, forests were cut down. Rivers that had been pristine became muddy because of the mining and timber industry. The wildlife declined. The ecosystem was altered in a way that was not fully understood. 

The expansion also had an impact socially. The areas identity changed. For instance, the frontier became more populated. There was a mix of people with different backgrounds. There were hopes for a bright future. However, not everyone benefited equally. 

By 1887, the eastern area of the southern Argos had changed from unknown land to a busy frontier. Trade routes were established. New industries were being developed. It was an important addition to the total economy. Industrial consolidation began. The wild growth of 1885-1886, when independent prospectors, small logging outfits, and scattered plantations dominated, was slowly coming to an end. Large companies and government-sponsored businesses began taking over the small operations, especially in the oil, gas, and mining industries. This meant less independent operators and more centralized control of resources.
 
Oil fields, once experimental, were becoming organized areas of oil extraction with permanent rigs, storage facilities, and guarded operations. At the same time, infrastructure growth was rapid and becoming more effective. What were once muddy paths were becoming reinforced roads. River transport was becoming more regulated, with checkpoint and toll areas. 

Early pipeline operations were becoming more effective, connecting oil areas with trade centers. Several frontier camps were becoming formally recognized as towns, with offices, supply depots, and basic government. In 1887, the displacement of people and the use of forced labor had become a breaking point. The groups of people pushed off their lands or into the plantation and industrial workforce had begun to fight back.  Uprising raids, sabotage of supply lines, strikes against isolated camps, and uprisings in labor camps. To counter this, more security measures were being taken. Troop strength was increased, patrols stepped up, and fortified camps were being erected around economic centers, especially oil fields and large plantations.[/i][/spoiler]
